newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Guerrilla Maskhadov likely Chechen president.
newsitem.headline: Guerrilla Maskhadov likely Chechen president.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who forced Russian troops out of Chechnya with a combination of guerrilla warfare and shrewd diplomacy, seemed almost certain to be its next president as votes were counted on Tuesday.

"There's a very great likelihood he'll go through in the first round," Bilal Ozdemirov, a member of the secessionist region's Central Electoral Commission, told reporters after 10 to 20 percent of Monday's ballots had been counted.
Maskhadov, a quietly spoken 45-year-old former colonel in the Soviet artillery, needs to win at least 50 percent of the vote to avoid a second-round run-off in two weeks.
Electoral Commission chairman Mumadi Saydaiyev told Russian Television Maskhadov had more than 60 percent by early morning. A preliminary result may be available towards evening, he said.

Moscow, which agreed to elections as part of a face-saving peace deal with Maskhadov, will be relieved if he beats Shamil Basayev, a hardline guerrilla commander wanted as a "terrorist" in Russia. Ozdemirov said Basayev, 32, was a distant second, ahead of acting separatist president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev.

In Moscow, President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia, called a meeting of his top-level Consultative Council to discuss the results of the poll on Tuesday. The council comprises the heads of the two chambers of parliament, the secretary of the Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, and the head of the presidential administration, Anatoly Chubais.

A very high turnout on Monday, which forced officials to extend polling by two hours to cope with long queues, may lend weight to Maskhadov's call for the Kremlin to recognise demands for sovereignty from the mainly Moslem Chechen people.

Some electoral officials estimated turnout could reach 70 percent or more of the half million or so electorate. Precise figures are unreliable as tens of thousands of war refugees no longer living in Chechnya were bussed in to vote.

Outside observers have said they were impressed by the smoothness of the voting and an absence of major violations. The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) will make an official report late on Tuesday.

Leading Russian human rights activist Sergei Kovalyov told Russian Television: "The elections were held correctly." But he repeated his criticism that many refugees, especially ethnic Russians, living further afield, were unable to vote.

There were no reports of violence despite Chechen accusations that Russian special forces might seek to discredit the poll by staging "provocations". Chechen leaders accused Russian special services of being behind the unexplained killing of six foreign Red Cross workers in December.
Moscow vehemently denies the charge.
Maskhadov has pledged to work with those guerrilla leaders, including Basayev, who opposed him during the election and to prevent Chechnya sliding toward Afghan-style anarchy.

He won a reputation in Moscow last year as the rebel leader most open to compromise after 21 months of fighting. But Maskhadov, who masterminded the stunning guerrilla victory last August, has made no less solemn pledges than Basayev to secure Chechen sovereignty after 200 years of Russian domination.

He wants international recognition of a Chechnya rebuilt with Russian "war reparations". Moscow has already promised, in the peace signed with Maskhadov last year, to provide massive aid to rebuild an economy based on oil refining and pipelines.
But many Russian politicians, especially in the communist and nationalist opposition condemned the accord and are pressing President Boris Yeltsin to save his money for Russia.
A Russian Deputy Foreign Minister said at the weekend that Moscow was ready to break off relations with any country that moved to grant Chechnya diplomatic recognition.

Yeltsin admits sending troops to crush the Chechen rebels in 1994 ranks as one of the biggest mistakes of his presidency. It could be one that haunts him well into a second term already overshadowed by illness.
Chechens in their devastated capital Grozny voiced mixed emotions about the prospect of Maskhadov as their leader.
"I think that today Maskhadov is the best man to stabilise the situation in Chechnya," said one young man.
"Now they (Russia) will have to recognise us, we're people too, like Portugal, Holland, we're not monkeys," said another. "With Maskhadov as president everything will be OK."
But another armed man sporting the black beard of a Moslem guerrilla, feared Maskhadov would be "too soft" on Moscow.
"He may be a soldier, but he's weak," he said. "The people who voted for Maskhadov are opposed to independence."
Maskhadov's task will be far from simple.
Chechnya has won de facto independence with the withdrawal of Russian troops. But with its back to the towering Caucasus mountains, it is hemmed in by Russian territory and is all but bankrupt.
